newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic faces new pressure on election results.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic faces new pressure on election results.

text.p: Shaken by six weeks of street protests, the Serbian government admitted on Friday that opposition parties had won some municipal elections later annulled by the ruling socialists.
But the pro-democracy opposition rejected the statement as a pack of lies and said it would maintain its massive daily street protests against President Slobodan Milosevic.

The United States blasted Belgrade for what it called Serbia's "hollow assurances" of a commitment to democracy. The admission also failed to satisfy the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which had investigated opposition claims of election fraud.
Serbian authorities made no mention of the biggest election prize, the Belgrade city assembly, and said results in several key towns including Serbia's second city, Nis, were unclear.
The admission by foreign minister Milan Milutinovic came in a written response to a report by the OSCE mission which investigated the disputed local elections.
The OSCE report endorsed opposition allegations that electoral fraud in the November 17 polls cheated it of victory in 15 of Serbia's largest towns, including Belgrade.
The United States issued a fresh warning that Belgrade's refusal to recognise the opposition victories would lead to further isolation.

State Department Nicholas Burns said in Washington that Milutinovic's response "does not go nearly far enough" and "fails to address seriously the recommendations" in the OSCE report that could help resolve Serbia's political crisis.
Burns said Secretary of State Warren Christopher had outlined the U.S. view in a "very tough" message to Milosevic.

Milutinovic's response also failed to satisfy the OSCE. At a special meeting on Friday, it affirmed that the Serbian opposition fairly won each invalidated election and called for complete recognition of the results by the authorities.

"The OSCE endorses the recommendations of (former Spanish prime minister Filipe) Gonzalez's report and calls for prompt and complete implementation," said Lars Vissing of Denmark, whose country took over the OSCE chairmanship on January 1.

Serbia's pro-democracy Zajedno (Together) coalition rejected the government's ambivalent message as a pack of lies and vowed to continue with daily mass protests until its victories were reinstated in all disputed districts.

Dissension over the annulment of the elections has surfaced in the army, the Serbian Orthodox Church and even the security police, all mainstays of autocratic leftist government in federal Yugoslavia since 1945.
In his letter to the OSCE, Milutinovic said the government conceded Zajedno won a majority in nine wards of Belgrade.
But he said nothing about the Yugoslav capital's policy-making municipal assembly and maintained the outcome in Nis, the original hotbed of protests, was still uncertain.
"When competent authorities establish the facts, the results of the elections (in Nis) will be known," he said.
He acknowledged Zajedno won three other cities and no party captured a majority in three others, and called for more data on six other municipalities at issue.
Gonzalez found evidence of vote-rigging and concluded that Zajedno had won every municipal vote subsequently invalidated.
In a statement, Zajedno blasted the Milutinovic letter.

"It makes patently clear that ... Milosevic not only rejects Gonzalez's report and OSCE recommendations but also deliberately misleads the world about the election results in Serbia," said the statement, faxed to news agencies.
"It has become very clear that Milosevic has opted for a conflict with the whole world in an effort to stay in power."

Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno leader who would have become Belgrade mayor if the Socialists had yielded power, warned Milutinovic's letter "will make the demonstrators even more angry. It shows that the regime has lost its compass".

Endorsing his comments, tens of thousands of whistle-blowing protesters massed in a Belgrade square for the 47th consecutive day. They dispersed without violence after riot police blocked them from marching into a busy main street.
But at 7:30 p.m. sharp, the city errupted in noise as protesting Belgraders leaned from windows and balconies blowing whistles and banging pots for the second night running.
The opposition has called for the nightly protest to "drown" the official television news bulletin which Zajedno says routinely distorts its reports of the protests or ignores them altogether.
